kb.admin-login-fails.cause: Two common causes: 1) misspelled config field — the correct field is `adminApiKey` (not adminKey; someone once changed the correct assertion to the wrong one, exactly backwards); 2) the Admin routes are only mounted when admin_api_key is non-empty — without it the whole section is absent.
kb.admin-login-fails.problem: Opening /admin fails to log in, or calling /api/admin/* always returns 401.
kb.admin-login-fails.solution:
1. Check config.json: the field must be named `adminApiKey` and non-empty.
2. Log in with that key (new versions store the key in sessionStorage, cleared when the tab closes; just log in again).
3. `adminApiKey` takes effect immediately after PUT /config (auth_keys hot reload, no restart); the old key dies at once. Conversation traffic uses a different key: `apiKey`.
4. Confirm you're hitting the right path: /admin is the UI, /api/admin/* is the API; both share `adminApiKey`.
kb.admin-login-fails.title: Panel login fails / admin API 401
kb.all-pool-cooldown-429.cause: Every upstream 429 puts the matching credential into tiered cooldown (normal rate-limit 15s, suspicious activity 20s, upstream 5xx 30s, auth failure 3600s without auto-recovery, etc.); with a small pool, all credentials cooling at once shows up as a whole-pool 429. Historical measurements showed that half of the panel's "rate-limited 38%" was actually an empty/fully-disabled pool, not real rate limiting.
kb.all-pool-cooldown-429.problem: Requests start returning 429 in batches; the error says all credentials are cooling down, or "all credentials disabled (0/N)".
kb.all-pool-cooldown-429.solution:
1. Open the panel's "Credentials" page and check each credential's cooldown reason and remaining duration (AuthenticationFailed / AccountSuspended / QuotaExhausted do not auto-recover).
2. Credentials in cooldown will recover automatically; zombie credentials in cooldown (auth-failure class) can be recovered with "Reset" or relogin in the credential actions.
3. If it says "0/N all disabled", go through the credentials page, check each disable reason, re-enable or add credentials.
4. Check the trace: if credential_id is NULL and retry_after_secs=10, no upstream request was ever sent — the problem is the pool, not rate limiting.
kb.all-pool-cooldown-429.title: Requests return 429 in bulk (whole pool cooling down) — what to do
kb.arch-family-collateral.cause: The health circuit breaker's key = family_key: M365 same tenant → m365:{tenant}, AWS same account → aws:{account}; when one credential hits account-level risk control the whole family backs off together (by design, prevents hammering them one by one); IdC/social/api_key → cred:{id}, each independent, no collateral.
kb.arch-family-collateral.problem: One credential hit account-level risk control — why does the whole group slow down / back off?
kb.arch-family-collateral.solution:
1. The panel's health score aggregates per family; same-family credentials drop together.
2. To isolate risk, split same-tenant credentials across different family_keys.
3. Note: a bare-429 health key historically used cred:{id}, which meant M365 credentials never tripped the breaker (fixed — uses family_key_of).
kb.arch-family-collateral.title: Family collateral: whole tenant family backs off
kb.arch-hot-reload.cause: TIER1 (ArcSwap atomic mirror) covers cooldown/rate-limit/affinity/RPM/load balancing etc., immediate; TIER2 (background task abort+respawn) covers token pre-refresh, balance refresh interval; TIER3 (process-level mirror) covers extract_thinking/compression/strip_env_noise. Honest boundary: prompt_cache_ttl / proxy / tls / port still need a restart. `apiKey` and `adminApiKey` hot-reload via auth_keys and take effect immediately after PUT /config.
kb.arch-hot-reload.problem: Some config changes apply immediately, others need a restart — how to tell?
kb.arch-hot-reload.solution:
1. Changing proxy/tls/port requires a restart. `apiKey` / `adminApiKey` do not (panel save rotates them; the old key dies at once).
2. Change config through the panel's PUT /config (hot-reload dispatch), don't edit the config file directly and restart.
3. Note: the socks auto-health switch is in-memory (resets to default true on restart); config.json has no field for it.
kb.arch-hot-reload.title: Three-tier hot reload: which configs take effect immediately, which need restart
kb.arch-request-chain.cause: Chain: security layer (IP whitelist/rate limit) → CORS/Body → auth (constant_time_eq) → conversion (Anthropic→Kiro) → compression (against 5MiB) → scheduling (affinity → selection → retry/failover) → upstream event-stream → SSE return → usage into pipeline. Selection is a 12-key ascending sort inside one lock's critical section (unusable sink, starved anti-starvation, health tier, ramp tier, whitelist hit, inflight, model call count, capacity permille, RPM used ratio, p_avail, success_count tiebreak).
kb.arch-request-chain.problem: From a request arriving to the final response, what happens in between? How is a credential chosen?
kb.arch-request-chain.solution:
1. Troubleshoot layer by layer: whether the trace has credential_id, what error_message markers say, where latency sits.
2. For selection anomalies, check sort-key semantics first: inflight only enters the key, no hard gate (prevents fake queueing); catch-all credentials staying behind saturated whitelist ones is deliberate explicit-routing priority.
3. Priority mode shares the same keys (prio_first semantics unchanged).
kb.arch-request-chain.title: Full request chain and 12-key credential selection
kb.arch-usage-pipeline.cause: Design decision: the sink does synchronous blocking IO (SQLite execute / writeln!), so on tokio workers it would be eroded by slow-disk/fsync jitter and spread latency back into the request path — hence a dedicated OS thread, with the request path doing only one non-blocking try_send; when the channel is full it drops + AtomicU64 counter; sink panics are isolated with catch_unwind.
kb.arch-usage-pipeline.problem: Why doesn't usage accounting slow requests down? Can data be lost?
kb.arch-usage-pipeline.solution:
1. Panel usage numbers can lose tail records under extreme traffic (drop-when-full is deliberate; the counter is inspectable).
2. SQLite has busy_timeout 5000 and batch writes (wave 1); dual-instance concurrent writes no longer silently lose records.
3. If a trace is missing, first check whether the pipeline ever hit full.
kb.arch-usage-pipeline.title: Usage pipeline: dedicated OS thread + drop-when-full
kb.arch-v1-vs-cc.cause: /v1 sends message_start immediately (input_tokens is an estimate); /cc/v1 buffers message_start with BufferedStreamContext and waits for contextUsageEvent to get exact input_tokens. Claude Code depends on message_start.usage.input_tokens for its context progress bar and needs exact values, so Claude Code uses /cc/v1.
kb.arch-v1-vs-cc.problem: What's the difference between the two message endpoints, and which should clients use?
kb.arch-v1-vs-cc.solution:
1. Claude Code → /cc/v1; generic SDKs → /v1.
2. Both endpoints share the same security/conversion/scheduling/compression logic; only the stream context differs.
3. The ccAutoBuffer switch affects whether /v1 also uses the buffered variant.
kb.arch-v1-vs-cc.title: /v1 vs /cc/v1: input_tokens precision
kb.auth-keys-hot-rotate.cause: src/common/auth_keys.rs keeps two process-level keys: `apiKey` authenticates downstream /v1 (and /cc/v1) conversation traffic; `adminApiKey` authenticates /admin and /api/admin. PUT /config seeds the setters immediately — no restart. Empty storage always fails closed (blank key does not open the gateway); setters refuse empty writes. After rotate, the old key dies at once.
kb.auth-keys-hot-rotate.problem: Are the conversation client key and the panel login key the same? Does changing them need a restart? Does the old key still work?
kb.auth-keys-hot-rotate.solution:
1. Conversation clients use `apiKey` (x-api-key / Bearer); panel login uses `adminApiKey`. Do not mix them.
2. Change either under Settings → Network and save; no restart. The old key returns 401 immediately.
3. Do not set either to empty — empty storage is fail-closed (all requests denied), not fail-open.
4. Editing config.json without PUT /config does not update the hot cells; that path still needs a restart.
kb.auth-keys-hot-rotate.title: Two keys: apiKey vs adminApiKey, hot rotate
kb.backup-restore.cause: Data lives in three places: config and credentials in the config volume (config.json / credentials.json / .at_rest.key), usage detail in the data volume (traces.db / usage-*.jsonl), and the previous binary at kirostudio.bak. config.json auto-rotates keeping 3 .bak copies before each write.
kb.backup-restore.problem: Worried that an upgrade or config change will break the service; need to know where data lives and how to back up / restore.
kb.backup-restore.solution:
1. Before upgrading, confirm both `./data` and `./config` volumes are mounted (container deployment), and keep the previous binary/image tag.
2. After a crash, check `docker inspect <container>` for the restart count (RestartCount field) growing, confirmed with `docker compose ps`.
3. Restore = stop → point the image tag back to the previous version → up -d; for config corruption, restore config.json from its .bak rotation.
4. The at-rest key (.at_rest.key) must be kept separate from ciphertext (see security article).
kb.backup-restore.title: How to back up and restore (read before upgrading)
kb.cfg-alert-webhook.cause: With alertWebhookUrl configured (+ alertCooldownSecs default 600s), key self-heal events (absorb budget exhausted / all failover credentials dead / retry quota exhausted / 429 storms) POST {key, value, window_secs, host} to that address; the same key is sent at most once per cooldown window, repeated events within the window only accumulate counts. Hot-reload doesn't apply (injected at provider construction) — restart after changing.
kb.cfg-alert-webhook.problem: How to configure alert pushes? Why doesn't a change take effect?
kb.cfg-alert-webhook.solution:
1. Changing alertWebhookUrl requires a service restart.
2. Security: the gateway sends requests to that URL — prefer an internal-unreachable, externally-only alert service; never an internal management address (SSRF risk is on you).
3. Before changing alert text/status codes, grep external consumers (kiro_shield.py classifies by body text; 503 must contain COOLDOWN-related markers).
kb.cfg-alert-webhook.title: Alert webhook config: cooldown dedup + SSRF risk
kb.cfg-deliberate-deviations.cause: rateLimitEnabled=false: the per-credential 1000ms minimum interval would kick affinity bindings at 241ms → switching credentials every request → prompt cache fully lost, and measured correlation between rate and 429 rate is only +0.09 (doesn't stop risk control but kills caching); rpmHardGateOverloadWait=true (opposite of the code default false); all seven tool tolerance options on (including toolTruncationRecovery, default off — rather retry the whole round than send half-cut arguments); trustForwardedHeader=false (sub2api doesn't forward XFF, enabling it gets no real IPs and the IP blacklist would block all traffic).
kb.cfg-deliberate-deviations.problem: Which configs differ from code defaults in production such that reverting them causes real failures?
kb.cfg-deliberate-deviations.solution:
1. Before touching these switches, read the CLAUDE.md rationale and the ops repo docs/02-tuning.md.
2. Don't infer production behavior from code defaults.
3. Run a controlled experiment before changing rate-limit configs.
kb.cfg-deliberate-deviations.title: Production config deliberately deviating from defaults (don't revert)
kb.cfg-field-name.cause: The correct field is adminApiKey (serde camelCase, admin_api_key in src/model/config.rs). Someone once changed the correct assertion to the wrong one (exactly backwards); three independent readings confirmed: production config.json has adminApiKey and no adminKey, and both ops scripts read adminApiKey and work.
kb.cfg-field-name.problem: Configured adminKey but panel auth doesn't work.
kb.cfg-field-name.solution:
1. Write adminApiKey in config.json, not adminKey.
2. Before changing config-related docs/assertions, validate your correction like you'd validate the original assertion.
3. Read live production values before use; don't trust recorded numbers (credentialRpmLimit was recorded as 85/200, currently reads 100).
kb.cfg-field-name.title: Config field spelling check: adminApiKey, not adminKey
kb.cfg-semantic-traps.cause: 1) cooldownEnabled=false isn't "no cooldown" but "429'd credentials immediately re-selectable = thrashing in place"; 2) inboundQueueTimeoutPassthrough=true degrades the shaping layer into a delay (releases after 5s queueing), acting as amplifier lubricant for retry scripts; 3) inboundRpmAuto defaults true in code but production deliberately sets false (the built-in AIMD is a one-way ratchet: 429 halves the rate, recovery needs 20s of silence — measured one 429 per 6.4s → monotonic descent locked to the floor).
kb.cfg-semantic-traps.problem: Some switches look harmless but have opposite or surprising real consequences.
kb.cfg-semantic-traps.solution:
1. Keep cooldownEnabled true (turning it off = 429'd credentials immediately re-selectable, worse).
2. Keep inboundRpmAuto false; the external throttle-autotune script adjusts inboundTargetRpm every 2 minutes.
3. These traps are guarded by test_throttle_semantics (changing them turns it red).
kb.cfg-semantic-traps.title: Three semantic-trap switches: names don't match their real consequences
kb.chain.chain-alert.desc: Failure closure: 429/5xx/risk-control feed cooldown (tiered durations) and health scores (AIMD/family collateral) respectively; key self-heal events alert via webhook (cooldown dedup).
kb.chain.chain-alert.name: Alerting & cooldown
kb.chain.chain-auth-gate.desc: constant_time_eq verifies x-api-key / Bearer (empty key fail-closed), then the inbound shaping gate (token bucket; timeout 429 with Retry-After).
kb.chain.chain-auth-gate.name: Auth & inbound gate
kb.chain.chain-compress.desc: Whitespace folding + tool_result truncation; large requests trigger the compression retry loop (max 3, targets progressively harder, 64KiB floor).
kb.chain.chain-compress.name: Compression layer
kb.chain.chain-convert.desc: Anthropic → Kiro conversion: model mapping, three-state machine, environment noise stripping, continuationId derivation.
kb.chain.chain-convert.name: Conversion layer
kb.chain.chain-inbound.desc: Optional IP whitelist / per-IP rate limit (rightmost XFF segment) → CORS → body limit (256MiB default) → request enters the gateway.
kb.chain.chain-inbound.name: Client inbound
kb.chain.chain-select.desc: Session affinity → 12-key sort selection (inflight+1 + rpm.record atomic commit in one lock) → health/cooldown/whitelist hard-gate filtering.
kb.chain.chain-select.name: Selection & scheduling
kb.chain.chain-sse.desc: event-stream decode (dual CRC) → Kiro events → Anthropic SSE (message_start → deltas → message_stop) + thinking extraction + filter chain.
kb.chain.chain-sse.name: Response stream / SSE
kb.chain.chain-upstream.desc: Absorb layer (swallow 429 within budget so the client never sees it) → switch/failover (dynamic retry budget + 45s wall clock) → 403 region self-heal → AWS event-stream upstream.
kb.chain.chain-upstream.name: Upstream call & absorb retry
kb.chain.chain-usage.desc: Request path non-blocking try_send enqueue → dedicated OS thread → SQLite per-record + JSONL + in-memory pre-aggregation (drop when full + counter).
kb.chain.chain-usage.name: Usage recording
kb.connect-new-client.cause: The gateway serves Anthropic-compatible (POST /v1/messages, POST /cc/v1/messages) and OpenAI-compatible (POST /v1/chat/completions, POST /v1/responses) on a single port. The conversation key is config `apiKey` (x-api-key / Bearer); the panel login key is `adminApiKey`. Neither is an upstream credential, which is easy to mix up. There is no `/openai` route.
kb.connect-new-client.problem: A new client doesn't know how to reach the gateway: what address, key and format to use.
kb.connect-new-client.solution:
1. Open the panel's Connection info page (conn tab): Anthropic and OpenAI cards, each with curl/env examples, one-click copy.
2. Anthropic: set `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` to the gateway origin → client hits `/v1/messages`; for Claude Code exact input_tokens set `origin/cc` → `/cc/v1/messages`. OpenAI-compatible: `POST /v1/chat/completions` and `POST /v1/responses` on origin (no `/openai`).
3. Use config `apiKey` as the conversation API key (x-api-key or Authorization: Bearer) — not the panel `adminApiKey`, and not upstream Kiro credentials.
4. Browser/frontend direct access needs the CORS whitelist (corsAllowedOrigins) and inbound IP allowlist.
kb.connect-new-client.title: How to configure a new client (Claude Code / Cursor / SDK)
kb.cors-error.cause: The gateway's CorsLayer only allows origins in the corsAllowedOrigins whitelist; when your site's origin isn't in the default whitelist, the browser blocks the request.
kb.cors-error.problem: Frontend pages / browser extensions calling the gateway directly are blocked by browser CORS.
kb.cors-error.solution:
1. Add your origin (protocol+host+port, written out fully) to `corsAllowedOrigins` in config.json.
2. Confirm it's an Origin header mismatch, not a key problem (401 is auth; CORS errors are network-layer blocking).
3. Avoid `*`: combined with an adminKey leak it means full takeover, and it conflicts with CSP fixes.
kb.cors-error.title: Browser direct access fails with CORS errors
kb.credential-auto-disabled.cause: Auto-disable has several entry points: consecutive failures reaching the threshold (TooManyFailures), quota exhaustion (QuotaExhausted), account suspension (AccountSuspended), too many refresh failures, etc. The disabled state is persisted to disk and does not revive on restart (deliberate fix: prevents dead credentials from re-entering the pool after restart and burning repeatedly).
kb.credential-auto-disabled.problem: A credential in the panel shows "disabled" and no longer receives requests; it needs to be restored.
kb.credential-auto-disabled.solution:
1. Check the disable reason: TooManyFailures usually means a wrong region or a dead key; QuotaExhausted means insufficient balance; AccountSuspended means the upstream banned the account.
2. After the cause is resolved (top up, change region, confirm the key works), run "Reset failure count" (reset_failure_count) on the credential page.
3. Use the "Restore" action in the recycle bin for hard-deleted credentials.
kb.credential-auto-disabled.title: A credential was auto-disabled — how to recover
kb.deploy-crashloop-detect.cause: restart: unless-stopped restarts forever; a new version that crashes on startup shows as Restarting. Note that "process alive but degraded" is not a crashloop (that's the watchdog's domain).
kb.deploy-crashloop-detect.problem: A new version crashes on startup, showing as "restarting forever" — how to judge and handle?
kb.deploy-crashloop-detect.solution:
1. Three elements: RestartCount keeps growing (check twice, tens of seconds apart) + docker compose ps long-term unhealthy (after 90s) + log tail repeatedly showing the same crash point.
2. Handling: docker compose stop, point the image tag back to the previous version, up -d; for a corrupted config use config.json's .bak rotation.
kb.deploy-crashloop-detect.title: Crashloop judgment: three elements and rollback
kb.deploy-data-volumes.cause: Usage data (traces.db + usage-*.jsonl) lands in usageDataDir by default (relative to the process cwd); in the container WORKDIR is /app, so if compose doesn't mount `./data:/app/data`, a rebuild loses everything.
kb.deploy-data-volumes.problem: After a container rebuild, panel usage/success-rate reset to zero.
kb.deploy-data-volumes.solution:
1. Verify compose volumes include `- ./data:/app/data` (or point usageDataDir explicitly at a mounted directory).
2. Before upgrade/rebuild, confirm both `./data` and `./config` exist (first item of the upgrade checklist).
3. Health check: after upgrade, /healthz's sqlite_writable should be true.
kb.deploy-data-volumes.title: Data volumes: not mounting them means losing all usage detail
kb.deploy-diagnostics.cause: Three endpoints: GET /api/admin/diagnostics/snapshot (version/per-credential state/proxy pool health/self-heal counters aggregated in one shot, pure observation zero side effects), /api/admin/recovery-metrics (self-heal counters), /api/admin/endpoint-health (per-credential × endpoint measured success EWMA). All behind Admin API auth.
kb.deploy-diagnostics.problem: How to get the full state at once when troubleshooting?
kb.deploy-diagnostics.solution:
1. Troubleshoot starting with diagnostics/snapshot.
2. Pool/endpoint issues: endpoint-health and recovery-metrics.
3. The alert webhook consumes recovery_metrics counters (429 storms/budget exhaustion/all credentials dead/credential disabled).
kb.deploy-diagnostics.title: Ops observation trio: diagnostic snapshot / recovery metrics / endpoint health
kb.deploy-healthcheck.cause: The correct probe is /v1/models: both 200 and 401 count as healthy (401 means connection established, routing hit, auth interception working); /admin is a full UI page behind adminApiKey auth — probing it is heavy and doesn't reflect "gateway usable". There's also an unauthenticated GET /healthz (ok/version/config_loaded/pool_count/sqlite_writable) suited for reverse-proxy active probing.
kb.deploy-healthcheck.problem: The container keeps showing unhealthy while the service is actually fine; or the reverse.
kb.deploy-healthcheck.solution:
1. healthcheck probes /v1/models (grep -Eq ^(200|401)$).
2. Caddy/reverse-proxy active probing uses /healthz.
3. "hotswap status FAIL" may be a false alarm: verify with docker ps actual state + Admin API 200; the criterion is connection refusal, not a status word.
kb.deploy-healthcheck.title: Health probe: probe /v1/models, not /admin
kb.deploy-log-limit.cause: With no limit, json-file log driver grows logs indefinitely (the usage pipeline also writes files; logs are an extra stream).
kb.deploy-log-limit.problem: Container logs grow without bound and fill the disk, service malfunctions.
kb.deploy-log-limit.solution:
1. Add a logging section to compose: max-size 10m + max-file 5.
2. For systemd deployments journald's SystemMaxUse is the safety net; don't use StandardOutput=file: (no rotation).
3. When troubleshooting disk-full, check docker logs size first.
kb.deploy-log-limit.title: Unbounded logs fill the disk
kb.deploy-ota-selfupdate.cause: The downloaded binary must pass sha256 verification (checksum fetched directly from github.com, breaking the same-source poisoning RCE chain), atomically rename over the exe, back up .bak before replacing; the systemd ExecStartPre guard implements "new version crashes on startup → auto-rollback to old version", with the rollback decision at the systemd layer, not in a process that may already be crashed.
kb.deploy-ota-selfupdate.problem: How does OTA updating guarantee the downloaded binary is trustworthy and failures self-heal?
kb.deploy-ota-selfupdate.solution:
1. Manually verify release artifacts: recompute SHA256 and match the repo's published value.
2. Historical pitfalls: OTA once selected assets by OS but not architecture (macOS got a Linux ELF and died on the spot) — now enumerates all 6 OS×ARCH combinations; a tag inconsistent with the Cargo.toml version causes an infinite upgrade loop, now gated in release.yml.
3. ExecStartPre rollback keeps the last .bak — don't delete it.
kb.deploy-ota-selfupdate.title: OTA self-update security chain: sha256 + rollback loop
kb.image-upload-slow.cause: Historically, image processing (JPEG re-encode / magic-bytes validation) ran as blocking computation directly on tokio workers, eroding the async thread pool and spreading latency to all concurrent requests; fixed by moving it out with spawn_blocking. If it's still slow, the upstream itself is slow at image processing or the body is very large.
kb.image-upload-slow.problem: Requests with images are noticeably slower, or feel stuttery.
kb.image-upload-slow.solution:
1. Confirm the gateway version >= v1.1.0 (the image block_in_place fix is in this version).
2. Image bodies are limited by DefaultBodyLimit (256MiB default); oversized requests are rejected.
3. Image count is capped by image_dedup (MAX_TOTAL_IMAGES=20); a repeated identical image is replaced with a placeholder (normal behavior).
kb.image-upload-slow.title: Image requests slow / laggy
kb.mod.src-admin-router.role: Admin route assembly (authed routes + public OAuth callback); endpoint list in ARCHITECTURE §11.
kb.mod.src-admin-service.role: Admin business logic core: credential CRUD, balance cache, config hot-reload dispatch, three write paths under one lock, diagnostic snapshot, OTA tasks.
kb.mod.src-admin_ui-router.role: rust-embed embedded React SPA + login page background-image proxy (with SSRF protection + MIME whitelist).
kb.mod.src-anthropic-cache_fingerprint.r: Cache fingerprint simulator (cache chain Layer 3): pure in-memory longest-common-prefix hits + session isolation + TTL split.
kb.mod.src-anthropic-compressor.role: Input compression (whitespace folding + tool_result head/tail truncation), avoiding the upstream ~5MiB body 400.
kb.mod.src-anthropic-converter.role: Anthropic → Kiro format conversion (three-state machine) + environment noise stripping + continuationId derivation + model mapping.
kb.mod.src-anthropic-handlers.role: Request entry: POST /v1/messages and POST /cc/v1/messages; the same /v1 nest also serves POST /v1/chat/completions and POST /v1/responses (implemented under src/openai/). Streaming/non-streaming dispatch, WebSearch replay dispatch, compression retry loop, inbound gate calls.
kb.mod.src-anthropic-stream.role: Kiro event-stream → Anthropic SSE return (Stream/Buffered dual contexts) + thinking extraction + DSML/XML leak filtering.
kb.mod.src-anthropic-websearch.role: MCP WebSearch: fast path + mixed-tool replay loop (up to 5 rounds) + result block rendering. TTFB rework target.
kb.mod.src-common-alerting.role: Alert webhook: 8 self-heal event hooks, cooldown dedup + failure retry cap, pure-function triple tests.
kb.mod.src-common-fs_atomic.role: Atomic file writes (temp → fsync → rename); the safe write path for config/credential persistence.
kb.mod.src-common-secret_store.role: Credential at-rest encryption (XChaCha20-Poly1305) + key file management (.at_rest.key).
kb.mod.src-common-ssrf.role: Outbound URL SSRF protection: scheme validation, IP segment blacklist (incl. 6to4/IPv4-mapped), DNS pinning against rebinding, redirects disabled.
kb.mod.src-kiro-affinity.role: Session affinity (session_id → credential_id, TTL); steady-state requests reuse the same credential to keep prefix cache.
kb.mod.src-kiro-cooldown.role: 8 cooldown reasons + tiered durations + disk persistence (kiro_cooldown.json); one of the selection hard gates.
kb.mod.src-kiro-endpoint-.role: Upstream endpoint registry: IDE (runtime.{region}.kiro.dev, OAuth credentials) and CLI (q.{region}.amazonaws.com + X-Amz-Target, ksk_ credentials), bound per credential type, not interchangeable.
kb.mod.src-kiro-health.role: AIMD circuit breaker + EWMA health score + family collateral (family_key); p_avail feeds selection sort weight.
kb.mod.src-kiro-passthrough.role: Passthrough mode (custom_api credentials): zero-conversion byte passthrough + passthrough-level filters (DSML strip/thinking/empty-stream guard). 100% of production traffic goes through this path.
kb.mod.src-kiro-provider.role: Core proxy: retry/failover/absorb layer/inbound gate/client cache/dynamic retry budget. Calls token_manager for selection then hits upstream.
kb.mod.src-kiro-scheduling.role: InflightGuard (RAII in-flight count) + RpmTracker (60s rolling window); part of the atomic selection commit.
kb.mod.src-kiro-throttle.role: Inbound shaping token bucket (AIMD auto-RPM gate); home of the three semantic-trap switches.
kb.mod.src-kiro-token_manager.role: Multi-credential management core: selection (12-key sort), token refresh, affinity, disable/cooldown state, credential CRUD and recycle bin. The largest file in the repo, deliberately not split.
kb.mod.src-openai-.role: OpenAI compatibility layer (convert/handlers/types/mod): inbound POST /v1/chat/completions and POST /v1/responses plus usage accounting. No `/openai` prefix.
kb.mod.src-usage-.role: Usage pipeline: dedicated OS thread + SyncSender (drop when full), SQLite detail + JSONL + in-memory pre-aggregation dual sinks.
kb.model-unsupported.cause: Multiple gates: 1) the model isn't in the whitelist (allowed_models) and the credential isn't a catch-all, so selection blocks it; 2) the pool-wide model_blocklist (TTL 1800s) temporarily blocks a model; 3) optional modelMapping may rewrite the name (off by default). deepseek normalization is gone — there is no whitelist-aware rewrite gate. If the mapped name is unknown upstream, the request fails.
kb.model-unsupported.problem: A request for some model returns a "model not supported" style error (error_message contains model_unsupported_by_pool or 400).
kb.model-unsupported.solution:
1. Read the machine-readable marker in the error: model_unsupported_by_pool=1 means the whitelist blocked it (non-retryable; resending is pointless).
2. Explicitly add the model to the credential's allowed_models, or use a catch-all credential.
3. If model mapping (modelMapping) is enabled, confirm the target is recognized upstream, or enable the credential's "exemption" (modelMappingExempt).
kb.model-unsupported.title: Requested model not supported / blocked
kb.ota-check-fails.cause: OTA update checks hit a private GitHub repo and need environment variables KIROSTUDIO_UPDATE_REPO / KIROSTUDIO_UPDATE_TOKEN (when a token is detected, only GitHub direct is used, third-party mirrors are excluded to avoid handing the PAT to a middleman). The production update.env token is empty, so the panel button necessarily fails.
kb.ota-check-fails.problem: Clicking check-for-updates in the panel errors out, or says no update while a new version is known to exist.
kb.ota-check-fails.solution:
1. OTA reads the public repo dwgx/KiroStudio by default; no token needed.
2. Make sure KIROSTUDIO_UPDATE_REPO is not pointed at the retired private skiapi repo.
3. Auto-check is a settings toggle (otaAutoCheck; in-memory until restart).
kb.ota-check-fails.title: The panel's "Check for updates" keeps failing
kb.pit-ai-code-must-pass-ci.cause: Defect classes caught in practice: raw strings ending with a quote closing early, /// doc comments used on function parameters (not allowed in Rust), re-entry infinite loops after cap trigger, truncated results exceeding the contract, test helpers feeding bare strings to functions expecting JSON objects.
kb.pit-ai-code-must-pass-ci.problem: Agent-delivered code reports claim "logically consistent", yet there were 5 classes of real defects, all caught by CI.
kb.pit-ai-code-must-pass-ci.solution:
1. Any agent-delivered code goes through server CI before being trusted.
2. "Logically consistent" / "tests pass" claims only count with `test result: ok` visible.
3. Run key behaviors by name individually so filters don't swallow them.
kb.pit-ai-code-must-pass-ci.title: Workflow agent code must pass CI before it can be trusted
kb.pit-block-in-place.cause: Image JPEG re-encode/processing is CPU-bound synchronous computation that originally ran directly in async handlers, blocking worker threads and spreading latency to all concurrent requests. The code even self-labeled it "to be fixed".
kb.pit-block-in-place.problem: Requests with images occupied the tokio async thread pool; concurrent requests collectively slowed down.
kb.pit-block-in-place.solution:
1. Fixed: moved out of the workers with spawn_blocking / block_in_place (wave 1).
2. For any new CPU-bound or synchronous-IO operation, first decide whether to move it off tokio workers (precedent: the usage pipeline uses a dedicated OS thread).
3. When debugging "everything slows down under concurrency", check whether blocking computation was added to the hot path again.
kb.pit-block-in-place.title: Blocking computation ran directly on tokio workers (image re-encode)
kb.pit-capacity-fake-number.cause: Pool capacity = credentialRpmLimit × rpmHeadroomFactor self-multiplied (production 500×85%=422), while the measured sustained clean ceiling of a single credential is only 137 RPM; and with a single-credential pool, rpm_saturation_gate_active unconditionally returns false, so no rpm threshold has any effect.
kb.pit-capacity-fake-number.problem: The "pool capacity" shown in the panel/scripts is 3× off from actual throughput; tuning by it is tuning in a vacuum, and users feel "config can't be tuned at all".
kb.pit-capacity-fake-number.solution:
1. Before judging any rate-limit config's impact, confirm its branch is actually reached (with a single-credential pool the RPM gate is inert).
2. Tune with measured data (traces.db's ok_before_429 criterion: <100 → bad credential, >1000 and monotonically rising with RPM → real rate limiting), don't trust config arithmetic.
3. Run a controlled experiment before changing credentialRpmLimit.
kb.pit-capacity-fake-number.title: Capacity figures are fake: self-multiplied config numbers aren't measurements
kb.pit-compress-retry-deadlock.cause: The compression retry target formula was inverted: the correct descent is trigger × 3/4 → 9/16 → 27/64 (progressively harder), but the implementation did 27/64 → 9/16 → 3/4 (progressively larger) — the first retry compressed hardest and the later rounds produced bigger bodies that necessarily failed, so 3 retries had only 1 effective. This was a real defect found by review (P0-2 compression deadlock self-heal task).
kb.pit-compress-retry-deadlock.problem: After a large request triggers compression retries, only the first round works; the later rounds produce even bigger bodies, so the upstream CONTENT_LENGTH hard threshold rejects them again.
kb.pit-compress-retry-deadlock.solution:
1. Fixed: compress_retry_target is now an independent function with a 65536 floor, and guard tests assert the call sites.
2. Any change to compression-related code must keep the guard test `compress_retry_loop_uses_extracted_target_fn` passing (changing the formula/position deliberately turns it red).
3. New compression behavior must ship with behavior regression tests.
kb.pit-compress-retry-deadlock.title: Compression retry target sequence reversed: rounds 2 and 3 are necessarily ineffective
kb.pit-config-limit-vs-actual.cause: SWAP_MAX_ATTEMPTS=60 × client × gateway suggested 480×, but measured 19579 judgments all fell in the [passthrough] branch with zero swaps; that 60 was never touched. What actually applies is the 30s wall-clock budget (max 7 attempts). Changing SWAP_MAX_ATTEMPTS is a dead config; the thing to change is MAX_BUDGET_SECS.
kb.pit-config-limit-vs-actual.problem: Computed "worst 480× amplification" from config caps and changed config accordingly, but nothing changed.
kb.pit-config-limit-vs-actual.solution:
1. To judge a config's impact, first confirm its branch is actually walked, then talk about its value.
2. Of 34 rate-limit knobs, only 4 actually limit (two code constants + two concurrency caps); the rest are dead configs/semantic traps.
3. Production also has kiro_shield.py in front of the gateway doing whole-request retries (measured 5.6× amplification) — grep external consumers before changing client-visible 503 text.
kb.pit-config-limit-vs-actual.title: Config value caps ≠ actual amplification: confirm the branch is reached first
kb.pit-config-lost-update.cause: update_config / import_config / set_load_balancing_mode originally didn't share a single lock, so concurrency produced lost updates (historically the only persistence-error class).
kb.pit-config-lost-update.problem: When multiple entry points write config at the same time, the later writer overwrites the earlier one's changes; config silently disappears.
kb.pit-config-lost-update.solution:
1. Fixed: all three write paths now share config_write_lock.
2. Any new "write config" path must join the same lock (guard test_config_write_lock_covers_both_write_paths turns red otherwise).
3. When debugging "config change doesn't take effect / reverts", first suspect a concurrent write path missing the lock.
kb.pit-config-lost-update.title: Concurrent config writes lose updates (lost update)
kb.pit-disable-not-persisted.cause: report_quota_exhausted / report_account_suspended / report_refresh_token_invalid / report_failure only called save_stats_debounced after disabling, and StatsEntry has no disabled/disabled_reason fields, nor was persist_credentials called (the only exception was suspicious_activity) — the disabled state was never written to disk.
kb.pit-disable-not-persisted.problem: Credentials with exhausted quota / banned / expired refreshToken re-enter the pool as enabled after restart, re-run the disable flow, wasting round-trips and repeatedly triggering upstream errors.
kb.pit-disable-not-persisted.solution:
1. Fixed: persist_disabled_state is now a single choke point, and all 5 disable paths go through it.
2. Any new code path that disables a credential must use this choke point, or it will silently not persist again.
3. When debugging "credential revives after restart", first suspect a disable path not going through persist_disabled_state.
kb.pit-disable-not-persisted.title: Auto-disable not persisted: dead credentials revive after restart
kb.pit-doc-line-drift.cause: The whole-repo line count drifted 2.5× from the docs (35,800 → 90,032 lines); every file-level count is stale. Comment/implementation forks are everywhere: ABSOLUTE_MAX_TOTAL_RETRIES comment says 12 but the code has 4; the compression retry comment says the opposite of the actual formula; prompt_cache_enabled is a dead config while the comment's "default-off cuts CPU" code path no longer exists; config.rs comments describe the deleted cache_tracker behavior.
kb.pit-doc-line-drift.problem: Line numbers, constant values and structural descriptions in docs disagree with the actual code; locating/deciding by the docs leads to mistakes.
kb.pit-doc-line-drift.solution:
1. Before citing a line number, read it live (codegraph / cg.py stat), don't trust doc numbers.
2. Update related comments when changing behavior/constants/structure — comment/implementation forks are a source of incidents.
3. When a "doc assertion" contradicts code, trust code + tests and fix the doc (validate your correction like you'd validate the original assertion — someone once changed a correct fact into a wrong one).
kb.pit-doc-line-drift.title: Doc line numbers and comments drift: the cost of not updating comments
kb.pit-frontend-dist-bind.cause: Production /opt/kirostudio-src/admin-ui/dist is mounted read-only into the container (taking precedence over rust-embed); hotswap deploy only swaps the backend binary, so the frontend must be rebuilt and synced separately. Identical Vite content hashes mean the source didn't change, not that the build failed.
kb.pit-frontend-dist-bind.problem: Changed the frontend and redeployed, but the page didn't change; or wrongly concluded the build failed.
kb.pit-frontend-dist-bind.solution:
1. After changing admin-ui source: build dist on the server with node, then docker cp to overwrite /opt/kirostudio-src/admin-ui/dist.
2. Don't treat "dist unchanged" as a build failure or deploy failure.
3. Frontend builds must use pnpm (npm produces conflicting lockfiles).
kb.pit-frontend-dist-bind.title: Frontend dist is a bind mount: hotswap deploy only swaps the backend
kb.pit-guard-silent-green.cause: Three real pitfalls: 1) the marker literal the guard matches was written in a comment, so splitting production code at "first occurrence" cut too early and truncated the production section; 2) macro_rules! inside a function relied on capturing outer locals, but macro hygiene resolves identifiers in the definition context — the binding isn't visible, so the check effectively doesn't exist; 3) the guard's needle appeared in the test section's own literals, coincidentally satisfying the count (coincidental truncation).
kb.pit-guard-silent-green.problem: Tests are all green but the guard isn't actually guarding: deleting the protected code still passes, the guard is a no-op.
kb.pit-guard-silent-green.solution:
1. After writing a guard, do the break experiment: verify it actually turns red when the target is removed, and the break must be type-equivalent (e.g. change `let x = ...; if let Some(_) = x` — deleting the field outright won't compile and can't test the guard).
2. When comments/docs describe code markers, deliberately avoid the literal (build the needle at runtime).
3. Outer variables used by in-function macros must be passed as explicit arguments, not captured.
kb.pit-guard-silent-green.title: Guard tests silently green: comment literals, macro capture, slice anchors
kb.pit-local-build-impossible.cause: A MacBook Air with 8GB RAM can't complete a full Rust build, and the frontend rust-embed is embedded at compile time with dist in .gitignore, so a fresh clone always hits E0599; locally you'd test TLS branches the release build never reaches (Cargo.toml default = native-tls, opposite of production config).
kb.pit-local-build-impossible.problem: Local cargo build/test fails, and the errors are unrelated to code quality (rust-embed E0599 without admin-ui/dist, missing node_modules).
kb.pit-local-build-impossible.solution:
1. Verification always goes through the skiapi server Docker loop: snapshot (temp index) → scp → docker build --target builder → docker run with explicit cargo test --no-default-features.
2. All cargo commands carry --no-default-features.
3. Judge green only on `test result: ok. NNNN passed; 0 failed`.
kb.pit-local-build-impossible.title: Local 8GB machine can't build: must use the server verification loop
kb.pit-region-burn.cause: 403 AccessDeniedException: The bearer token ... invalid is the known signature of region mismatch (documented in three comments), but the hot path counted "wrong region" as "dead key" into failure_count; 3 strikes → TooManyFailures disable persisted; and ksk_ credentials without apiRegion written always take config.region.
kb.pit-region-burn.problem: After changing config.region, ksk_ API Key credentials are invalid in the wrong region; 3 consecutive 403s count as failures, auto-disable with persistence, and restart doesn't bring them back; worse, "auto-recover after successful re-probe" simply doesn't exist in code, so the credential freezes for 24h into a zombie.
kb.pit-region-burn.solution:
1. Fixed (apiKeyRegionAutoProbe, default true): on 403 bearer-invalid for api_key credentials, failure is no longer counted immediately; a background region probe is triggered, success writes api_region back, failure only then counts a failure.
2. Manual handling: explicitly set the correct apiRegion on the credential (credential field takes precedence over config.region).
3. Keep the region whitelist discipline: only whitelisted values may ever be spliced into the upstream host.
kb.pit-region-burn.title: Wrong region burns credentials: 3× 403 bearer-invalid → permanent disable
kb.pit-ssrf-guards.cause: The background proxy /admin/api/bg-img was anonymously reachable and echoed response bodies; historically three gaps existed: 1) 6to4 (2002::/16) embedding IPv4 bypassed the IP blacklist; 2) DNS rebinding TOCTOU (resolution swapped after validation); 3) the prefetch pool (third-party JSON sources) didn't validate MIME, echoing text/html as-is and allowing script execution — combined with plaintext adminKey storage it enabled full panel takeover.
kb.pit-ssrf-guards.problem: Outbound URL features like the login page background proxy were used to hit internal networks; 6to4 IPv6 was a bypass path; unbounded MIME once caused same-origin XSS.
kb.pit-ssrf-guards.solution:
1. Outbound URLs must go through the ssrf.rs unified defense: http/https only, validate every candidate IP (reject private/loopback/link-local/cloud metadata segments, including IPv4-mapped IPv6 and 6to4), pin DNS against rebinding, disable redirects.
2. Response-type proxies must enforce a MIME whitelist (images only return image/*).
3. Keep CSP + nosniff on all new response endpoints.
kb.pit-ssrf-guards.title: SSRF guard pitfalls: 6to4 bypass, DNS rebinding, MIME gap
kb.pit-strings-check-unreliable.cause: Compiler optimizations inline/merge/delete literals; a string not greppable in the binary doesn't mean the code isn't there.
kb.pit-strings-check-unreliable.problem: strings/grep can't find a just-added literal in the compiled artifact, so the change is wrongly judged as not deployed.
kb.pit-strings-check-unreliable.solution:
1. To verify a change is live: inspect the deployed snapshot's source (git show <tag>:<file> | grep), not the binary.
2. Or observe live behavior (trace fields, log markers) — more reliable than static checks.
3. Same class of unreliable checks: local python bracket-counting for syntax errors (char literals/lifetime annotations misjudged) — let rustc report the line.
kb.pit-strings-check-unreliable.title: Using strings to verify deployed changes — unreliable
kb.proto-event-stream.cause: Frame structure: prelude(12B: total_length + header_length + prelude_crc) + headers(variable, 10 value types) + payload + message_crc. All big-endian; dual CRC32 (ISO-HDLC); 16MB frame cap. The decoder is a self-implemented streaming zero-copy state machine (Ready/Parsing/Recovering/Stopped), single-byte-skip recovery on corruption, entering Stopped after 5 consecutive errors.
kb.proto-event-stream.problem: What does the binary protocol between the gateway and the Kiro upstream look like?
kb.proto-event-stream.solution:
1. Protocol-layer issues (garbled/stream interruptions): check decoder state and CRC error counts first.
2. Both endpoints (IDE via URL path, CLI via X-Amz-Target header + service root) share the protocol; credential types are bound and not interchangeable (measured 403 when swapped).
3. The self-implemented decoder is a design decision (no off-the-shelf Rust lib supports streaming zero-copy decode).
kb.proto-event-stream.title: AWS event-stream frame format and dual CRC
kb.proto-model-mapping.cause: Contains matching + version-less fallback: claude-sonnet-4-* → sonnet-4.5, opus 4.x → opus-4.x, haiku → 4.5; mapped into Kiro numeric IDs (sonnet=14, opus=13, sonnet-3-7=12, haiku=10). Model mapping (modelMapping) is a user-configurable global flat map + per-credential exemption; usage records both the original name and the mapped name.
kb.proto-model-mapping.problem: How do requested model names correspond to the model IDs the upstream actually uses?
kb.proto-model-mapping.solution:
1. The usage page can view usage by "requested model" or "upstream model" (dual accounting).
2. The settings page's modelMapping JSON card accepts mappings (value-type validated; illegal input won't submit).
3. Post-mapping no whitelist check happens (whitelist governs the original name); the exemption switch is the safety valve.
kb.proto-model-mapping.title: Anthropic ↔ Kiro model ID mapping
kb.proto-sse-sequence.cause: Standard sequence: message_start → content_block_start → content_block_delta×N → block_stop → message_delta → message_stop; Kiro upstream thinking content is embedded in text with <thinking> tags; with extract_thinking=true it is extracted into an independent ContentBlock.
kb.proto-sse-sequence.problem: The event order of streaming responses and how thinking blocks are presented.
kb.proto-sse-sequence.solution:
1. When a client parses abnormally, verify against the event sequence above.
2. Whether thinking becomes an independent block is controlled by extract_thinking (TIER3 hot switch).
3. The gateway also strips DSML markers and filters tool_use XML leaks (DeepSeek upstream scenarios); response text differing from raw upstream bytes is normal.
kb.proto-sse-sequence.title: SSE event sequence and thinking handling
kb.proxy-misconfigured.cause: Proxy config supports a global proxy and per-credential effective_proxy; the socks proxy pool has automatic health scheduling (probe every 5 min, auto-disable a node after 3 consecutive failures). If the proxy address is unreachable or the credentials are wrong, all outbound fails; after a node is auto-disabled it looks like "some requests fail".
kb.proxy-misconfigured.problem: After configuring a proxy, all requests fail, or some nodes fail repeatedly.
kb.proxy-misconfigured.solution:
1. Check the proxy URL format (supports socks5://user:pass@host:port with embedded credentials).
2. A changed global proxy needs a restart (proxy is restart-only); per-credential proxies can be hot-changed.
3. The panel settings page has a "socks pool health probing" switch (socksAutoHealth, in-memory) — when troubleshooting nodes being auto-disabled, check it first.
4. Test the node manually (e.g. curl through it) before blaming the pool.
kb.proxy-misconfigured.title: Wrong proxy config makes all requests fail
kb.request-feels-slow.cause: Requests with web_search mixed tools unconditionally go through the WebSearch replay loop (regardless of whether the model actually searches); the whole round is buffered and the response is only returned when the loop ends, so TTFB equals the sum of all rounds (up to 5), much slower than normal streaming. Inbound shaping queueing also adds latency when enabled (normal behavior).
kb.request-feels-slow.problem: Sometimes a request takes a long time before the first token appears, or feels stuck.
kb.request-feels-slow.solution:
1. Check the request's trace: requests hitting the websearch replay path show a significantly larger TTFB — known behavior of that path.
2. Clients that don't need search: remove web_search from tools to take the main streaming path.
3. A first-byte handshake rework for this path is planned (pending live validation); no config switch yet.
4. If it's not the websearch path, check whether inbound shaping (inboundRpmAuto / target RPM) is queueing requests.
kb.request-feels-slow.title: Requests noticeably slower (first token takes forever)
kb.res-cache-chain.cause: Research findings: 1) the upstream Smithy model has CachePoint and MetadataEvent.tokenUsage.cacheReadInputTokens, but this repo never parsed metadataEvent (silently dropped as Unknown), so the real signal may have been there all along; 2) the cache_read_input_tokens sent to clients is a locally estimated fabricated value injected unconditionally, and it also back-subtracts from the only accurate upstream figure input_tokens — pure-Chinese multi-turn conversations can trigger message_start.input_tokens=0; 3) asymmetric accounting (tool definitions go into the denominator but not the numerator) and the estimator's error sign differs between Chinese and English.
kb.res-cache-chain.problem: Can the panel's cache hit rate / cache_read numbers be trusted?
kb.res-cache-chain.solution:
1. When reading cache figures: cache_read is an estimate, not an upstream truth (the panel tooltip says so).
2. Don't treat "47% discount" as fact — disproven by 460k traces (no implicit prefix-credit discount upstream); don't make decisions on it.
3. Correct order: measure first (parse metadataEvent) before applying loss mitigation.
kb.res-cache-chain.title: Cache chain research: the real signal was never parsed, cache_read is a fabricated value
kb.res-capacity-truth.cause: Read-only measurement over 270k production traces: best sustained 5-minute zero-429 = 137 RPM; "successes before the first 429" is the decisive criterion (rate limiting can't trigger at the 9th request — credentials arrive already in one of two states); the region hypothesis was falsified with three independent evidences (RTT fingerprint + cross-region control + cross-verification of credentials reading apiRegion directly).
kb.res-capacity-truth.problem: How much RPM can a single healthy credential actually sustain? How to attribute 429 rates?
kb.res-capacity-truth.solution:
1. Bad-vs-limited criterion (one SQL): ok_before_429 < 100 → bad credential; > 1000 with 429% monotonically rising with RPM → real rate limiting.
2. 429 and 403 are two independent failure chains; don't explain one with the other (error_message strings are identical, not evidence).
3. The panel's "rate-limited" percentage mixes pool-empty/full-disabled cases — read the credential states, not just the percentage.
kb.res-capacity-truth.title: Credential capacity truth: 137 RPM per credential is the measured ceiling
kb.res-fingerprint-simulator.cause: Research + implementation: ported the kiro2cc-proxy fingerprint idea as a pure in-memory version (longest-common-prefix hit + session-isolated seed + TTL 5m/1h split + LRU eviction), wired into cache chain Layer 3; scope deliberately trimmed: no persistence / no background thread / commit only on success; two implementation pitfalls fixed: Layer 3 on non-streaming paths was swallowed by the Layer 2 slot (forced downgrade), and drifting tool block ids broke the hit chain (signature excludes id + JSON canonicalize).
kb.res-fingerprint-simulator.problem: How can the gateway simulate upstream cache hits to estimate cache benefit?
kb.res-fingerprint-simulator.solution:
1. The fingerprint hit-rate panel number comes from the simulator and estimates benefit, not upstream truth.
2. Fingerprint Layer 3 has a known undercount on non-streaming creation (MINOR, logged for decision).
3. Signature stability depends on ordered JSON keys (serde_json default BTreeMap — don't enable preserve_order).
kb.res-fingerprint-simulator.title: Cache fingerprint simulator (cache chain Layer 3)
kb.res-region-self-heal.cause: Research conclusion: synchronous region-swap retry sits inside user requests (3 round-trips + wall-clock cost), so adjudication must be async; failure counting must be deferred until the probe concludes; branches where the probe can't start must fall back to report_failure (prevent genuinely dead keys from becoming zombies); soft cooldown can't use AuthenticationFailed (86400s non-recoverable = panel shows a "cooling" zombie).
kb.res-region-self-heal.problem: How to handle 403 bearer-invalid credentials without burning them and without leaving zombies?
kb.res-region-self-heal.solution:
1. Implemented (apiKeyRegionAutoProbe, default true): 403 triggers a background probe; candidate set = own region → pool-verified regions (by success_count desc) → config region → fallback table, deduped to 3.
2. The three defenses are all required: probe-can't-start falls back to counting failure; probe success writes api_region back; probe failure counts failure.
3. Keep the whitelist: probe candidates are validated against SUPPORTED_KIRO_REGIONS.
kb.res-region-self-heal.title: Region self-heal design: async adjudication + pre-probe on pool entry
kb.res-unique-capabilities.cause: Five-way concurrent research: 7 unique capabilities — absorb layer (swallow 429 within budget so the client never sees it), shared budget (≤4 per request), family collateral (whole tenant family backs off), AIMD auto-shift, SSRF depth, at-rest encryption, zero-conversion passthrough; worth borrowing but not done: explicit model-channel routing, unified error normalization (model-level rate limiting and cost accounting landed in wave 2). `POST /v1/responses` inbound is live (same pipeline as `/v1/chat/completions`).
kb.res-unique-capabilities.problem: Compared with similar gateways (newapi / sub2api / all kiro.rs versions), where is KiroStudio stronger, and what's missing?
kb.res-unique-capabilities.solution:
1. When troubleshooting against upstream comparisons, first confirm whether a unique capability is in play: the absorb layer only covers the main path, not passthrough (with 100% passthrough traffic the absorb knobs do nothing).
2. Model-level rate limiting and the cost table are available in v1.1.0 (by-model cost column identifies money-burning models).
3. Explicitly-out-of-scope list (evidenced): newapi user/payment/distribution, Redis/MySQL, multi-tenant billing.
kb.res-unique-capabilities.title: Unique capabilities no reference repo has
kb.res-websearch-buffering.cause: Research conclusion: content can only be published per-round (replay-round text being invisible to the client is a protocol semantic, not implementation laziness), so true token-level streaming doesn't exist on this path; after comparing four plans, the reference-repo-verified "first-byte handshake" was chosen (ping + oneshot racing 200/error code): TTFB returns to the upstream first-chunk level, content still batches per loop, plus an enhanced ping after each round.
kb.res-websearch-buffering.problem: Mixed requests with web_search have TTFB equal to the whole loop duration — how to fix?
kb.res-websearch-buffering.solution:
1. The rework is designed (render_deferred_sse skeleton referenced from ref-grey @795b9ca), to be implemented after live validation.
2. Don't aim for token-level streaming — replay-round content isn't publishable, that's a protocol constraint.
3. Keep the run_web_search_loop function name (two source-level guards anchor it).
kb.res-websearch-buffering.title: WebSearch replay path TTFB rework design (plan C chosen)
kb.sec-at-rest-backup.cause: credentials.json can enable at-rest encryption (XChaCha20-Poly1305); the key .at_rest.key (32 bytes, 0600) lives in the same directory as the credentials. Packaging the whole directory as a backup carries key and ciphertext together = backup leak means full credential decryption (access_token/refresh_token/api_key/proxy_password all decryptable).
kb.sec-at-rest-backup.problem: With at-rest encryption on, how to back up / migrate safely?
kb.sec-at-rest-backup.solution:
1. Backup packages may include credentials.json (ciphertext), but .at_rest.key must be kept separately (e.g. a password manager), never inside the credential backup.
2. Whole-directory backup scripts should first exclude .at_rest.key.
3. Losing the key = ciphertext permanently undecryptable: before migrating/deleting keys, export plaintext credentials from the settings page.
4. Windows backup tools that zip the directory silently include hidden dotfiles — audit the archive contents.
kb.sec-at-rest-backup.title: At-rest encryption: the key must be separated from ciphertext in backups
kb.sec-auth-fail-closed.cause: Design decision: blank apiKey refuses to start, preventing fail-open anonymous consumption (strangers connecting and burning upstream quota for free). Auth uses constant_time_eq constant-time comparison against timing attacks.
kb.sec-auth-fail-closed.problem: Why does the service refuse to start when apiKey is empty in config?
kb.sec-auth-fail-closed.solution:
1. api_key must be non-empty for the service to start.
2. Auth failures return 401; clients should switch keys rather than blindly retry.
3. When IP whitelist/per-IP rate limit are all unset, no middleware is mounted (zero overhead); they only apply once configured.
kb.sec-auth-fail-closed.title: Auth fail-closed: empty apiKey refuses to start
kb.sec-csp-session.cause: Historically: adminKey stored plaintext in localStorage + no CSP anywhere + background-proxy MIME gap = complete takeover chain. Fixed: CSP header + adminKey moved to sessionStorage (cleared when the tab closes) + background-image MIME whitelist + nosniff. At-rest encryption doesn't resist a local attacker (design boundary).
kb.sec-csp-session.problem: After a panel XSS, what can an attacker get?
kb.sec-csp-session.solution:
1. The panel key lives in sessionStorage, cleared when the tab closes; re-login after reopening is normal.
2. New response endpoints must keep the CSP/nosniff and MIME-whitelist discipline.
3. Background processes (same account) can read in-memory keys; at-rest encryption only protects "ciphertext copied away", not a local attacker.
kb.sec-csp-session.title: CSP header and adminKey session storage (the last piece of the XSS takeover chain)
kb.sec-region-whitelist.cause: Credential region/auth_region/api_region + IdC onboarding region must pass the SUPPORTED_KIRO_REGIONS whitelist; poisoned values are no longer spliced into the upstream host (otherwise refresh_token could be POSTed to an attacker's domain).
kb.sec-region-whitelist.problem: Can a malicious region in a credential send requests to an attacker's domain?
kb.sec-region-whitelist.solution:
1. When hand-editing credentials.json, only use whitelisted region values.
2. Onboarding flows (idc/region probing) carry their own whitelist validation.
3. When troubleshooting requests hitting a strange host, first check whether the credential region passed the whitelist.
kb.sec-region-whitelist.title: Region whitelist: preventing poisoned values from entering the upstream host
kb.sso-token-paste.cause: The add-credential dialog has an SSO Token tab: paste the AWS portal session Bearer Token (header x-amz-sso_authn). The server POSTs /api/admin/credentials/import-sso, runs the device-auth flow, and inserts a standard IdC credential. Server poll is up to ~120s. The token is single-use in-process and is not persisted.
kb.sso-token-paste.problem: Already signed in at the AWS portal and don't want the IdC device-code / browser flow — how to import the account into the pool?
kb.sso-token-paste.solution:
1. After signing in at the AWS portal, copy the x-amz-sso_authn Bearer Token from browser devtools.
2. Open Add credential → SSO Token, paste it, and confirm region (default us-east-1; a wrong region fails auth).
3. Wait for the server exchange (up to ~2 minutes). The token is used once in this flow and is not saved.
4. This is not the Microsoft External IdP three-step path, and not IdC device code.
kb.sso-token-paste.title: How to onboard by pasting an SSO Token (no browser grant)
kb.stale-balance.cause: Balance goes through a backend cache (balance_cache) refreshed periodically, and the cache is shared per account key; the panel shows the cached snapshot rather than a live query, to avoid hitting upstream on every view. Seeing a stale value within the refresh interval is by design.
kb.stale-balance.problem: The balance figure stays unchanged for a long time, or doesn't match actual charges.
kb.stale-balance.solution:
1. Click "Refresh balance" on the credential to trigger a manual refresh.
2. Check the balance cache timestamp in the panel's top-left to confirm the refresh task (respawn_balance_task) is running.
3. If it stays stale for a long time, check backend logs for balance refresh errors (e.g. token expiry).
4. The overage auto-disable (autoDisableQuotaExceeded) depends on the balance cache; a stale cache can delay the disable.
kb.stale-balance.title: The balance shown in the panel is stale
kb.test-kiro-path.cause: Passthrough-first routing (should_try_custom_api_first): as long as the pool has custom_api credentials, requests unconditionally prefer them and the Kiro main path is never entered. This is designed behavior, not a bug.
kb.test-kiro-path.problem: Sending /v1/messages to test Kiro/WebSearch behavior produces no Kiro-path log lines; trace credential_id entries are all authMethod=custom_api credentials.
kb.test-kiro-path.solution:
1. Check the trace's credential_id → authMethod to see which path the request actually took.
2. To force the Kiro path: temporarily disable all custom_api credentials.
3. Or use a request signature that deterministically hits Kiro (e.g. auto-fallback when the whole custom_api pool is cooling).
kb.test-kiro-path.title: Testing the Kiro path but zero log hits (requests diverted to passthrough)

settings.absorb.budgetSecsHint: Floor is 45s (the existing failover wall clock). Smaller values are raised by the backend: a round is capped at min(45s, remaining budget), so below 45 it would also truncate ordinary credential-failover retries.
settings.absorb.capacity400Hint: Capacity-class issues (e.g. INSUFFICIENT_MODEL_CAPACITY) recover in minutes; this is the second layer after slow retries are exhausted. Off by default.
settings.absorb.enabledHint: Retry recoverable 429s in-gateway while the client has received zero bytes
settings.absorb.exhausted503Hint: Cursor kills the session on 429 but retries on 503; 503 is the safe default (changed 2026-08-11), check to return 429 instead. Affects only requests that actually ran through absorption and gave up.
settings.absorb.maxRoundsHint: ⚠️ Each round gets a fresh full failover retry quota (currently 4/round), so N rounds is worst-case (1+N)×4 upstream calls from one egress IP. This is part of why absorption ships off; read the code note before raising it.
settings.absorb.serverErrorHint: 502 is the dominant failure mode of relay upstreams (observed: router.denzao.com returns 'Upstream service temporarily unavailable'). Not absorbing it hands the most typical transient fault straight to the client. Unlike the 403 case, 5xx usually self-heals within seconds, so retries have a high success rate.
settings.absorb.suspended: Also absorb 403 temporary suspension (not recommended, conflicts with self-heal backoff)
settings.absorb.swapBudgetSecsHint: The account-swap gap (banned → auto_disable → next credential → push re-add) is ~10 minutes. >0 switches that class to the long ladder (20/40/60s) with its own deadline; 0 keeps the shared budget and short backoff curve.
settings.absorb.title: Upstream 429 absorption

absorb.budgetGapWarn: Absorption is off by default and one known defect is not fully fixed: the default 45s budget is below the 60s whole-pool self-heal backoff, so the "entire pool cooling" class is never absorbed (fix in progress).
absorb.maxDelayHint: Upper bound for a single wait. A larger upstream Retry-After is clamped to this value so one wait cannot consume the whole budget.
absorb.minDelayHint: Minimum gap between retry rounds. Set 0 to add no extra wait and follow the upstream Retry-After directly.
absorb.noEffectAllCustomApi: These settings currently have no effect. The absorb layer only applies to the Kiro upstream path and does not cover the custom_api passthrough path. Every enabled credential in the pool is a custom_api relay, so all requests go through passthrough and the options below are inert. To make them take effect, the pool needs a usable Kiro credential (ksk / OAuth).
absorb.suspendedHint: Also absorb upstream "account temporarily suspended" errors. These usually take minutes to clear, so absorbing them makes a single request wait a long time; enable only when client timeouts are generous.
absorb.warnShield: If something in front of the gateway already retries automatically (shield / Caddy), absorbing again inside the gateway multiplies with it (outer attempts × inner rounds) rather than adding. Consider turning this layer off, or lowering the outer retry count as well.
absorb.warnTitle: Check these two things before enabling

throttleProfile.desc: Configure the whole retry/throttle chain at once. A profile only fills in options you have not set manually; values you configured are never overwritten.
throttleProfile.directHint: Clients talk to the gateway directly. Inbound shaping passes requests through on queue timeout (prefer slow over rejected); the absorb layer is on so the gateway handles more and clients see fewer errors.
throttleProfile.manualHint: Every throttle option comes from your own config; the profile changes nothing. This is the default.
throttleProfile.shielded: Behind an external retry proxy (recommended for production)
throttleProfile.shieldedHint: Something in front of the gateway (shield/Caddy) retries automatically. Inbound shaping returns 429 on queue timeout instead of passing through, so the proxy honours Retry-After; cooldown is enabled so rate-limited credentials actually back off. Goal: keep outer retry amplification from reaching upstream.
throttleProfile.title: Throttle profile

schedulingMode.title: Scheduling
schedulingMode.desc: Pick by how you use the gateway. Personal clients talking to it directly → Smart. A large relay with Caddy/shield retrying in front → Stable. You want every knob yourself → Manual.
schedulingMode.smartHint: Personal / direct: 1–3 credentials, clients talk to the gateway themselves. The gateway handles retries and cooldown so clients see fewer errors.
schedulingMode.stableHint: Large relay: many credentials, with Caddy/shield retrying in front. Queue timeout is a real 429 and cooldown stays on, so outer retries do not stampede upstream.
schedulingMode.manualHint: Expert knobs: no preset is written; every control below stays as you set it. For troubleshooting or fine-tuning.
schedulingMode.dailyOnly: Day to day, these three presets are enough.
schedulingMode.confirmDesc: Switching writes the preset parameter matrix: manually tuned values in the advanced area are overwritten (explicitly configured ones are kept), and cooldownEnabled is set to true — the live config currently has it false, which means rate-limited credentials never back off.

settingspage.advanced.cache.enabled.hint: On: responses carry cache_read_input_tokens and clients such as Claude Code display "N tokens read from cache". Off: the field is omitted entirely rather than set to 0 — for Anthropic clients 0 means "genuinely no hit", a missing field means "this gateway does not account for it". Either way the dashboard and SQLite keep recording the estimate.
settingspage.advanced.cache.estimateNote: This number is estimated locally by the gateway, not reported by upstream. In a 20-probe run all requests returned 200 and every metadataEvent carried only stopReason, with zero hits on tokenUsage / cacheRead*. Responses are tagged with x-kirostudio-cache-estimated: true — do not use this number for cost accounting.
settingspage.advanced.cache.mock.enabled: When on, passthrough pool responses carry a simulated cache read value (cache_read = upstream input × ratio) for downstream display / billing reference; when off, upstream values are passed through untouched. Independent of the prompt cache accounting above (accounting uses the estimate path, this uses the passthrough path).
Inject mock cache reads into passthrough responses
settingspage.advanced.cache.mock.ratio.h: Injection ratio (0–100%, default 70%). 100% injects a full cache_read on every passthrough based on upstream input.
settingspage.advanced.cache.nativeEffort: Off by default. When on, extended thinking for Opus 4.8/4.7 (five tiers incl. xhigh) and Opus 4.6/Sonnet 4.6 (four tiers) is delivered via upstream output_config.effort instead of XML tags (only the former triggers upstream reasoningContentEvent). Models outside the whitelist are unaffected. Ported 2026-08-11, not verified on live upstream — off by default is deliberate.
settingspage.advanced.cache.noSavingsCla: How much it saves: there is no credible figure. The repository holds two contradicting measurements (one shows roughly 47% credit discount on an identical prefix, the other shows no implicit prefix cache) and adjudication is still open, so no savings number is shown here.
settingspage.advanced.cache.ttl.label: Cache estimate TTL
settingspage.advanced.cache.ttl.value: Not exposed here: the current estimator is stateless (prefix tokens are recounted per request), there is no expiring cache table, so changing the value alters nothing.

settingspage.advanced.selfHeal.base.hint: Base seconds for pool-wide self-heal backoff (default 60). Controls how often suspended accounts are retried after upstream 403 bans — too small re-hits the wall, too large recovers slowly (history: 36 triggers in 41 min).
settingspage.advanced.selfHeal.max.hint: Backoff ceiling in seconds (default 900 = 15 min); together with the base value it caps the exponential ladder.
settingspage.advanced.selfHeal.max.label: Self-heal max backoff (s)
settingspage.advanced.selfHeal.shift.hin: Exponential shift cap (default 4). Each consecutive failed heal doubles the wait until this cap; any success resets the streak. Must be <32 (consumers clamp at 31).
settingspage.advanced.subtitle: Tool-call resilience / 429 absorption / prompt cache accounting. These switches change how the gateway behaves toward upstream and clients; a wrong value causes real outages, so the group is collapsed by default.

settingspage.advanced.tool.offCount: {n} of the seven are currently off, which deviates from the production recommendation.

settingspage.advanced.toolCompat.hint: On by default. When on, Claude Code's 8 built-in tools (Write/Edit/Bash/Read/Glob/Grep/LS/WebSearch) are mapped to Kiro native names and parameters (fs_write/str_replace/...), fixing `Invalid tool parameters`; when off, built-in tools pass through untouched (long-name shortening only), for non-Claude Code clients or custom tools that happen to share the names. settingspage.cliAlign.desc: Make ksk_ API Key requests look closer to the real kiro-cli client. All three are off by default, so behavior is byte-identical to before. ⚠️ All four reference implementations send these values, but none has controlled-experiment data showing they reduce 429 or ban rates — enable on a single credential and compare 429 rates before rolling out pool-wide.

Off (default) sends true, refusing training, at the cost of differing from the real client.

settingspage.export.desc: Export credential tokens as full JSON (re-importable), refreshToken-only text, or copy to clipboard. Includes sensitive fields such as refreshToken / kiroApiKey — keep them safe.
settingspage.export.toast.noRt: This credential has no refreshToken (may be API Key auth)
